quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable; the certificate names parents and birthplace, resolving the birthplace conflict. Image check of the original is the verification step.

Patrick's own burial entry (Catholic parish burial register, cemetery or obituary) after the 1908-03-12 death. loc_001 says sacramental registers are held at the parish and the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection is name-searchable; burial entries often state age and birthplace, and the cemetery plot may place him beside Thomas Flynn.

The 1850 census (log_001, log_002) found Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84; ages are only indirect evidence. The 1860 census (S2 is cited in the tree) and 1870 track the household; 1880 records relationship to head and birthplace of each person and of parents. Check whether Patrick is still with Thomas and whether the mother and siblings are named. Cover the later window through 1880 and 1900.

Baptism of Patrick, if born in Pennsylvania. SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (1708-1985) is name-searchable; Catholic registers are under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not Scranton, per loc_001. Search Flynn spellings (Flinn, Flin, Flynne, Fleming) and Patrick; the tree gives Ireland as birthplace so absence here points to an Irish birth and the death, marriage and naturalization items.

It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. If married in Ireland, it will not be found here.

FAN item: baptisms, marriages and burials of Patrick's probable siblings and of the neighbors near dwelling 84 in the 1850 census, and godparents or sponsors. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

The tree says Patrick was born in Ireland, so the plan also tries to find where the family came from.

Next, I will search the death certificate and then the census and church records for the Flynn family.

---

## What the tree already shows
- Katharina Seeger (I1) has one known fact: birth about 1843, Baiersbronn, Württemberg.
- She has no relatives, no attached sources, and no FamilySearch ark.
- The question's rationale references an 1855 Massachusetts State Census — that's an unverified emigration lead and is included in the plan.

---

## Where her parents would be recorded
Katharina's parents would most likely appear in the **Protestant church books of Baiersbronn**, which are held on **Archion** (a paid subscription site — not on FamilySearch). These are the core record types to search:

---

## Research Plan pl_001 — in order

| Step | Record | Where | What to look for |
|------|--------|-------|-----------------|
| **pli_001** | Baptism registers, 1840–1847 | Archion, Baiersbronn | A baptism entry for Katharina names both parents directly. Try spellings: Seeger, Seger, Segger, Säger; Katharina, Catharina, Katarina |
| **pli_002** | Familienregister (family register) | Archion, Baiersbronn | Lists a couple with all their children |
| **pli_003** | Parents' marriage record, 1815–1843 | Archion, Baiersbronn | Confirms parents as a couple; may give mother's maiden name |

| **pli_006** | Siblings' baptisms & godparents, 1835–1870 | Archion, Baiersbronn | Corroborates the parents and identifies other children |
| **pli_007** | 1855 Massachusetts State Census | FamilySearch | Tests the unverified emigration lead |
| **pli_008** | German indexes & family trees | MyHeritage | Leads only — verify any findings against Archion originals |

---

## What you need to do

**For the Archion items (pli_001–006):** You will need to browse these yourself since it's a paid site. Start at the Baiersbronn parish page:

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

# Locality Guide: Feliciana Parish / East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana (1810-1835)

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. This is a geographic split: which successor parish holds a given record depends on where within the old parish the event occurred, and that is frequently unknown. Records for a family resident in the old parish before 1824 may be found under either successor's name after that date — search both.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

sources.title: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Deed Records, 1875, Patrick Sheahan purchase
sources.citation: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Recorder of Deeds, Deed Book 42, p. 118, Patrick Sheahan from James Kelly, 1875; FamilySearch digital images.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree survey: Michael has a 1870 Residence in Pennsylvania (county outside Schuylkill, farmer, per log_001) and a 1882 Schuylkill Residence with Occupation Miner (log_002). The 1880 US census (name-searchable) falls between them and shows whether he was still farming elsewhere or already in Schuylkill, his occupation, household and neighbors; it tests the 'around 1882' date and whether the change was work-driven. It also gives relationship to head.

FAN item. Tree survey: brother Patrick Sheahan (I2) bought land in Schuylkill County in 1875 from James Kelly (Deed Book 42 p. 118, S1). A brother settled there seven years before Michael's 1882 appearance points to a kin-pull as a possible reason, alongside or instead of mining. Read the deed and look for other Sheahan or Kelly transactions, including any naming Michael. Per loc_001 laborers often leased from mining companies, so no Michael deed is not negative evidence.

FAN and subject item. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Search Michael and Patrick Sheahan (variants Sheehan, Shehan, Sheean) for marriages, baptisms of children, sponsors and burials, which show parish, timing of arrival and the kin and neighbor network. Per loc_001 registers sit with the parish or Archdiocese of Philadelphia, so follow hits to the parish.

The 1900 US census (name-searchable) is later than the move but records occupation, birthplace, and for immigrants year of arrival. It tests whether Michael stayed in mining and his household and neighbors, and shows whether he was a migrant from elsewhere in the US or abroad. Records created after the window testify to the move.

Direct test of mining employment: coal company payroll and employment records, mine inspector annual reports and local city directories for 1880-1890 may list Michael by colliery. Holdings and access are not known from tools this session, so the researcher or search-external-sites must locate the repositories (Pennsylvania State Archives, regional historical societies) on their own sites. A colliery employment record would document the work reason directly.

Local coal-region newspapers of the period reported colliery openings, hiring, strikes and arrivals, and notices naming the Sheahans. They give context for why labor was drawn to the county in the early 1880s and may name Michael or relatives. Repository access must be located via external newspaper archives.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill register of wills and the 1870 home county. An estate or will of the Sheahan parent (unnamed, I3) or of Patrick may name Michael's residence and relation. Window set by the parents' and Patrick's plausible lifespans (to about 1930), not Michael's move date.

Michael's own naturalization (if he was foreign-born; unverified) or other court filings. Per loc_001 coal-region naturalization films are browse-only, so browse images. Declarations state origin and arrival and may name witnesses who are fellow miners or kin. Lower priority.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Intervening link: log_001 (1870, farmer, outside Schuylkill) and log_002 (1882 directory, miner, Schuylkill) leave 1870-1882 undocumented. United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable; it shows whether Michael was already in Schuylkill in June 1880 (move earlier than 1882), still a farmer elsewhere, or already a miner, and gives birthplace, relationship to head and household members. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan, Shean variants statewide, then Schuylkill.

FAN item. The tree records Patrick Sheahan (brother, same parent I3) resident in Schuylkill in 1875 via a deed from James Kelly (Deed Book 42, p. 118, S2). That suggests Michael may have followed his brother rather than simply a job. Plan Recorder of Deeds entries naming Patrick, Michael or James Kelly as grantee, grantor or neighbor. loc_001 notes laborers often leased coal-company land rather than buying, so absence of a Michael deed is expected and not negative evidence.

FAN item. Locate Patrick Sheahan's 1880 household in the 1880 census (name-searchable): his occupation, neighbors and any co-resident Michael or other boarders show whether the brother was in mining and whether Michael joined that household or neighborhood, which tests a kin-chain motive alongside the mining one.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers stay with the Philadelphia diocese/archdiocese and parish, not the county. Baptisms of Michael's children, his marriage, or sponsors who are Sheahan kin or mining-town neighbors fix his parish and first years there and may name an origin. Use spelling variants.

Michael's own marriage, if after arrival: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 are name-searchable. Entries give residence, occupation and birthplace/parents; a miner's occupation and witnesses on the record add evidence of the work. Pennsylvania civil death registration began 1906 (loc_001), so also search Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (name-searchable) for his occupation, birthplace and parents if he died after 1906.

United States Census, 1900 and 1910 are name-searchable and record relationship to head, occupation (miner, laborer, foreman), months unemployed, immigration year and naturalization status, showing whether mining was a sustained livelihood after the move. Reaches past the 1882 window deliberately.

Local coal-region newspapers (Pottsville and nearby towns, e.g. via Chronicling America or Newspapers.com) report collieries opening, hiring, strikes and labor demand around 1882, and may mention Sheahan by name. This tests the cause (demand for miners) and gives context; it cannot show Michael's own motive unless he is named. Origin county of Michael is unknown, so also check papers there for a departure notice once the 1880 census names it.

Occupation-specific records: colliery and coal company payrolls and employment ledgers, and Pennsylvania Inspector of Mines annual reports for Schuylkill districts, plus fatal accident lists. These are the only records that could directly document employment by a named company; hold sites (Pennsylvania State Archives, local historical societies, Hagley) must be identified on their own sites. Fallback if Michael is not named: use the lists to establish that firms were hiring in 1882.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse Schuylkill Register of Wills images for wills or estates of Michael, Patrick or a Sheahan parent (a parent can die decades later, so the window follows their lifespans, not the 1882 move). Heirs, residences and mining-related claims or accident settlements may state where the family came from and why.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F3 records Michael as a miner in Schuylkill County in 1882 (log_002, a directory); log_001 shows him a farmer in 1870 outside the county. United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and is the nearest census to the move; it records occupation, birthplace, relationship to head and months unemployed, and names neighbors and co-boarders who may be fellow miners. Search Sheahan with variants Shehan, Sheehan, Shehen, Sheahen. A date before 1880 in the county would place the move earlier than family tradition's 1882.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. loc_001 notes Catholic sacramental registers stay with the parish and the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, and the surname suggests but does not prove an Irish Catholic family (unverified). Baptisms of children, marriage entries and burials would date his first appearance in a coal-region parish and may name a prior residence. Use the surname variants listed in item 1. Some coal-region church films are browse-only per loc_001, so browse the parish images if the name search fails.

Direct evidence of employment: anthracite colliery or coal company payroll and employment ledgers, and the state mine inspectors' annual reports naming collieries and workforces, would show whether and where Michael worked underground and from when. Locate the holding repository (state archives, county historical society, Pennsylvania anthracite collections) through its own catalog, since no tool here returned a specific location. The 1882 directory gives no employer, so start with collieries near his 1880 residence from item 1.

Local coal-region newspapers (e.g. Pottsville-area papers) report colliery openings, hiring, strikes, accidents and arrivals of new families. They can show whether mine labor was being recruited around 1880-1882 and may mention Michael or a relative directly (accident or injury notices are common for miners). Provides context for the move and a possible direct mention.

log_001 found Michael as a farmer in 1870 in a county outside Schuylkill; re-read that household and its neighbors. FAN item: relatives, in-laws or neighbors in the origin household who later appear in the coal region would indicate a chain migration and the source of the job. Also confirms the origin county, which the project tree lacks (F1 records only Pennsylvania), so later 1880 and church hits can be matched on more than name.

loc_001 says the Recorder of Deeds holds land records from 1811 and that much coal-region land was leased from mining companies, so laborers often bought a house lot or left no deed. A purchase or sale of a lot, or a lease, would show settlement timing and who he dealt with. Also check the origin county for a sale of his farm around 1880-1882, which would show he left farming deliberately. Negative results are meaningful here.

Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 is name-searchable. If Michael or a son married in the county, the entry gives occupation, residence and often birthplace and parents, evidence of the household's mining ties. Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 is a companion collection. Pre-1906 civil birth and death registration did not exist per loc_001, so marriages are the main civil source for this period.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and records occupation, birthplace, immigration year if foreign born, and years married. Shows whether he stayed in mining and who lived with him. The 1890 census schedules are largely lost, so 1900 is the next census after 1880. Dated after the 1882 window but testifies to continued mining work.

Michael's own death entry: Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable and gives occupation (often miner, with cause such as miner's asthma), birthplace, parents and length of residence in the locality, which can date the arrival. His death may predate 1906, in which case use the church burial in item 2 and cemetery records. Window set by his plausible lifespan.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill county Register of Wills, not a name search. An estate file or will could name heirs and kin elsewhere, and a miner's injury or employer settlement may appear. Window runs to roughly 1940 to cover his plausible death.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Tree facts: the 1850 and 1860 censuses (S1, S2) place Patrick (age 5, then 15, Ireland) in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill household; the 1908 death certificate (S3) names Thomas as father but gives Pennsylvania as birthplace. The 1870 census (United States Census, 1870, name-searchable) should show Patrick, about 25, either still with Thomas or heading his own household. Search Flynn with variants Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Patrick/Pat, and age 23-27, also in adjoining anthracite counties. A 1870 census names no relationships, so a shared household is indirect evidence only.

The 1880 census (name-searchable) is the first to state relationship to head of household, so a Thomas Flynn (about 62) listed as father or father-in-law in Patrick's household, or Patrick listed as son in Thomas's, would be the first direct census statement of the relationship. It also gives parents' birthplaces, which test the Ireland versus Pennsylvania birthplace conflict. Use the same name variants; Patrick would be about 35.

The 1900 census (name-searchable) records birth month and year, years married, immigration year and parents' birthplaces, and relationship to head. The 1890 census schedules were largely destroyed, so 1900 is the only later enumeration before Patrick's 1908 death. Thomas (born about 1818) would be about 82, so look for him in Patrick's household as father; if absent, it bounds his death between 1880 and 1900 and directs the probate item. Also check Patrick's household for the son-in-law James Brown (informant on the death certificate).

ps_001 names Thomas Flynn's probate as an unsearched gap. loc_001 says the county Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811, a primary source naming heirs. Window is sized to Thomas's likely lifespan (born about 1818, so death plausible from 1860 to about 1905), not to Patrick's life; census results in items 1-3 narrow it. A will or administration naming Patrick as son would be direct evidence. Check FamilySearch Pennsylvania probate first, then the courthouse.

Dedicated parents' marriage item: Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's maiden name (census and death records omit her), and, by date relative to Patrick's birth about 1845, corroborate the father otherwise named only by indirect evidence. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Tree gives Ireland as the birth place, so the marriage may be in Ireland or in an early Pennsylvania Catholic parish (registers held by parish or diocese, Diocese of Philadelphia per loc_001). Allow for a remarriage: if the 1880 or 1900 households show a wife of another surname, add her other marriages.

Patrick's own burial entry and obituary. A baptism may not exist: loc_001 notes statewide registration began only in 1906 and church films are partly browse-only, and Patrick's birth (Ireland per the censuses) predates any known register for him. Parish burial register, cemetery record or obituary may state age, birthplace, parents or surviving family. Complements the death certificate, whose informant was a son-in-law.

FAN item. Use the 1870, 1880 and 1900 findings to identify neighbors and other Flynn households adjacent to Thomas and Patrick, plus Patrick's son-in-law James Brown and Patrick's siblings. Their marriages, obituaries or probate may name Thomas as father or grandfather, and a sibling's record naming the same parents tests the parentage independently.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.description: Patrick Flynn's birthplace: Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) vs. Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate)
items.independence_analysis: The two census records (1850, 1860) are independent original sources with different enumerators. The death certificate is a third independent original source. However, the census informants are likely the same household member (Thomas Flynn or wife), so the two census assertions may share a single informant — potentially not fully independent for this fact.
items.weighing_analysis: The census records are contemporary recordings made near the time of Patrick's birth, while the death certificate was created 63 years later. The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.
items.resolution_rationale: Ireland is accepted as the birthplace. The 1908 death certificate birthplace of 'Pennsylvania' is rejected as a likely error by the son-in-law informant, who may have confused Patrick's place of residence with his place of birth, or may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland before immigrating as a young child.

entry.rationale: Closes the gap named in ps_001. Tree records Patrick b. ~1845 and Thomas b. ~1818, both Ireland, from the 1850/1860 censuses (Patrick age 5 in 1850, age 15 in 1860, in Thomas's household). The 1870 schedule (United States Census, 1870, name-searchable) should show whether Patrick, now ~25, still lives with Thomas or has his own household. It names no relationships, so it is corroboration only. Search Flynn/Flinn/Flin/O'Flynn variants.

The 1880 census (name-searchable) is the first to record relationship to head of household, so it can state directly whether any Flynn household member is son or mother of the head. Look for Thomas (~62) with a Patrick in the household or an elderly Thomas/wife in Patrick's household. Check birthplaces of parents, which 1880 records for each person, to test the Ireland versus Pennsylvania birthplace conflict (c_001). Use Flynn spelling variants.

A will or administration of Thomas Flynn would list heirs and could name Patrick as son, the direct evidence ps_001 says is missing. Window is set by Thomas's lifespan (b. ~1818, alive in 1860, could die anywhere to ~1908), not Patrick's. loc_001 says the county Register of Wills holds probate from 1811. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill county volumes, not a name search. Also check any estate of Thomas's wife and Patrick's own estate (d. 1908, son-in-law James Brown informant) for named heirs and siblings.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) to Patrick's presumed mother. It would confirm them as a couple, may give her surname (unreliable as her birth name if this was a remarriage, so do not call it her maiden name until tested), and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates the father otherwise named only by census co-residence and a secondary death-certificate informant. It does not by itself show Patrick is their child. Thomas was born in Ireland and Patrick's birth is placed in Ireland, so the marriage may lie in Ireland and be unreachable here. Search Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (both name-searchable), and the Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable), without presuming a surname for her. Companion test: the sibling and heir records in the church and probate items name the mother directly.

FAN and sibling item. Baptisms of other Flynn children born to Thomas in Schuylkill after immigration would name both parents and the mother's maiden name, and place Thomas's family in a parish. Loc_001 notes Catholic registers stay with the parish and diocese (Philadelphia), not the county. Search Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn as father and for households adjacent to dwellings 84 (1850) and 112 (1860) as possible kin or sponsors. If a parish register is unindexed, browse the parish's images.

Patrick's own burial entry. His birth window ~1845 may fall before any record reachable for him: the tree and ps_001 place his birth in Ireland (1850/1860 censuses), so no Pennsylvania baptism is likely and the death certificate (already searched, log_005) is the only end-of-life record in use. A parish burial entry or cemetery record, dated March 1908 (tree death 1908-03-12), in the parish where he last lived may give age, birthplace or parents. Use Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) and cemetery or obituary notices, naming son-in-law James Brown's family as leads.

Patrick's own marriage record (he was ~20-45 in this window). Marriage entries often name parents and a birthplace, independent of the secondary death-certificate informant. Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (name-searchable) covers later years only; for earlier years use Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and the church records. Witnesses are FAN leads.

The 1900 census (name-searchable) records Patrick near the end of life with birthplace of his parents and immigration year, which tests the Ireland birthplace and father's origin. Also shows co-resident in-laws such as the Brown household. Named as a remaining gap in ps_001.

Patrick was ~16-20 during the Civil War. United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865 (name-searchable) could show service; a service or pension file, which may be filed decades later, can name parents or a mother as dependent claimant. Pension and any muster records testify to events inside the window and run past it, so the date range follows the collection and not the question window. Only a lead until identity is confirmed by age and residence.

Mode: add-new. I marked the finished plan pl_002 completed and wrote a new active plan, pl_003. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Already recorded (survey)**
- Tree I1, Patrick Flynn: born ~1845 in Ireland (1850 census); died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (death certificate). He has no FamilySearch ark, so no hints item was planned.
- Tree I2, Thomas Flynn: born ~1818 in Ireland, linked as Patrick's father from the 1850 and 1860 censuses and the 1908 death certificate. The census entries give no relationships. The death-certificate informant was the son-in-law James Brown, a secondary informant.
- ps_001 rates the parentage "probable". The 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and Thomas's probate are listed as unsearched. Conflict c_001 accepted Ireland as the birthplace over Pennsylvania.

**Plan pl_003, in execution order** (all items are `planned`, none is a fallback, and all are on FamilySearch)
- pli_006, census, Schuylkill, 1870: shows whether Patrick still lives with Thomas.
- pli_007, census, Schuylkill, 1880: the first census with relationship to head, and it records parents' birthplaces.
- pli_008, probate, Schuylkill, 1850-1910: Thomas's will or administration naming heirs. The window follows Thomas's lifespan. The collection is `browse-only (personCount 0)`, so this is an image browse.
- pli_009, vital_record, 1835-1850: the dedicated marriage of Thomas to Patrick's presumed mother. It makes no claim about her maiden name and carries a note that it may have taken place in Ireland.
- pli_010, church, 1846-1865: baptisms of Thomas's other children and neighbours of dwellings 84 and 112. This is the FAN item.
- pli_011, church and cemetery, 1908: Patrick's own burial entry. No Pennsylvania baptism is likely because he was born in Ireland.
- pli_012, vital_record, 1865-1890: Patrick's own marriage, which may name his parents.
- pli_013, census, 1900: Patrick's parents' birthplaces and his in-laws' household.
- pli_014, military, 1861-1930: a Civil War service or pension lead, with the date range sized to the pension collection.

About nine searches. I skipped the wiki record-type pages: the subject was born in the British Isles and has no compound surname, so neither trigger applied. Irish-origin records are not planned because there is no locality survey for Ireland. If the researcher wants to trace Thomas's origin in Ireland, a locality survey is needed first.

Next step: hand the FamilySearch items to search-records, starting with pli_006.

---

This plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. The evidence so far points to a man named Thomas Flynn. It rests on two census entries that do not state relationships and on a death certificate whose informant was Patrick's son-in-law. The new searches look first at the 1870 and 1880 censuses to see whether Patrick still lived with Thomas. They then look for a will or estate file from Thomas, which would name his heirs, and for Thomas's marriage. After those come church baptisms of other Flynn children, Patrick's own marriage and burial, the 1900 census, and any Civil War service or pension file. Together these should show whether Patrick was Thomas's son and who his mother was.

Next, I will search these records in order, starting with the 1870 census in Schuylkill County.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Birth registration did not start until 1906 (loc_001), so baptisms are the main birth evidence. Collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable. Search baptisms with father John Doyle and mother Bridget Halloran (variants Hallorán, Holloran, Halloren, Bridgett, Biddy; Doyle/Doyl/Doil). Catholic registers sit with the Diocese/Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, not the county. Years run from a first child about 1855 to the 1879 remarriage to Martin Kearney (log_001). Ellen Doyle's parents are recorded as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran (log_003).

Dedicated search for John Doyle and Bridget Halloran's marriage to each other (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900, both name-searchable; County Marriages from 1885 is too late). It confirms them as a couple and dates the union, bounding when their children could be born. It does not by itself prove any child is theirs. Bridget is estimated born about 1838 in Ireland (tree F1). Also check the church marriage register (item 1 collection).

1860 US Census (name-searchable) should place John and Bridget Doyle with their earliest children, with ages and birthplaces. Pre-1880 schedules give no relationships, so children are inferred from household position and are leads only. Check variant surnames and neighbors on the page.

1870 US Census (name-searchable): the household of John and Bridget Doyle at the height of child-bearing, listing children who died before 1880 in the count of 9 (log_002). Also tests whether John was still alive.

1880 US Census (name-searchable) is the first to record relationship to head. Look for the Kearney household (Martin and Bridget, remarried 1879 per log_001) with Doyle stepchildren, and for Doyle children living apart as boarders or servants. Also search for John Doyle's widow-headed household if he died before 1879.

Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse Schuylkill Register of Wills docket images, not a name search. Look for John Doyle's administration or will (he apparently died before 1879), with heirs, guardianships of minors, and Bridget Kearney's or Martin Kearney's estate. Window is sized to the creators' lifespans: John to about 1879, Bridget probably to about 1925. The Register of Wills holds these from 1811 (loc_001). Heirs named would list living and deceased children.

Death certificates (name-searchable) post-date 1906. They are the subject's own death entry for Bridget, whose baptism cannot exist (born in Ireland about 1838). They also cover the surviving child other than Ellen and the 1900 count of 2 living children (log_002). They give parents' names and informant, who is often a child. Search Bridget Kearney and Ellen's sibling, and Ellen herself, for a sibling informant.

The 1900 Kearney household was read for fertility columns only (log_002). Search the 1900 and 1910 censuses (both name-searchable) for Ellen's household and the second surviving child, to identify that sibling and see co-resident relatives and neighbors (FAN). The 1910 census may show Bridget living with a child.

Children who died in infancy never appear in censuses. Check Find a Grave, BillionGraves and parish cemetery records in the coal region for Doyle burials in the same plots as John Doyle, Bridget Kearney or Ellen. Church burial registers (item 1 collection) too. Family plots reveal the other children among the 7 to 8 unidentified.

FAN-directed: obituaries for Bridget Kearney, Martin Kearney, Ellen (Doyle) and her husband usually list survivors and predeceased children. Coal-region papers (Pottsville and others) on Chronicling America, Newspapers.com, GenealogyBank. Also Ellen's marriage witnesses and sponsors at siblings' baptisms point to relatives.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

The question names death certificates. Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (1417491) is name-searchable. Tree holds only birth c.1814 (Kentucky) and a 1870 Muhlenberg residence, and loc_001 says statewide certificates begin 1 Jan 1911, so a certificate exists only if he lived to age 97+. Search name variants (Wilkins/Wilkerson/Wilkens, Elijah/Elisha) with Muhlenberg residence to test this quickly; a null result is expected and itself tells us the death was pre-1911.

Pre-1911 substitute for certificates: Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (1804888) is name-searchable. loc_001 notes county registers for 1852-1910 but partial 1860s-1870s coverage. Last known alive 1870 in Muhlenberg, so search 1870-1910; check neighbouring counties as well, since he may have moved.

loc_001: probate is the primary death evidence for the era; Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (1875188) is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse Muhlenberg County will/order books, administrator bonds and settlements for 1870 onward. Wills and estates bracket the date within months and localize the death to the county. Window runs to 1910 because a man b. c.1814 could die as late as the 1890s-1900s and settlements follow the death.

Tree's last record is the 1870 residence. The 1880 census gives relationship to head and marital status; absence from 1880 (or a widow listed in 1880) brackets the death window and confirms identity by age and birthplace. Check 1900 too (the 1890 schedules were largely destroyed) in case he survived.

Church burial registers and cemetery records (Find a Grave, county cemetery surveys) can state death or burial dates and place; loc_001 lists them as supplements when the county register is missing. Use as corroboration and as bracket if probate is silent.

FAN item: the death certificates (1911 onward) of his adult children or widow, found through the 1870/1880 household members, can name Elijah Wilkins as father with birthplace, and sometimes the father's death. This tests identity and the place he lived, supporting the identity part of the objective. Window set by the children's lifespans, not his.

Obituaries or death notices in Muhlenberg County papers, plus Kentucky Historical Society holdings, can give exact date and place and name survivors; a fallback if the registers and probate do not yield a date.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: The tree records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, citing Pennsylvania Death Certificates (S3), but not what the certificate says about his parents. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable; read the image for father's and mother's names, birthplace and informant. Informant-supplied parent data is secondary information. Starting-point note: the tree gives birth ~1845 in Ireland while the question says Pennsylvania; the certificate's birthplace helps settle that.

A baptism may not exist: if Patrick was born in Ireland ~1845 his baptism is outside Pennsylvania registers, and civil birth registration in PA began only 1906 (loc_001). His own burial entry, cemetery record and obituary (county newspapers) often give age, birthplace and relatives, and name the Catholic parish and family plot where Thomas may lie. Searched via Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) and Find a Grave.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (tree: born ~1818, Ireland) to Patrick's mother. It would confirm them as a couple, give the mother's name (a maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so test for earlier or later marriages; do not assume the surname is her birth name), and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Marriage may have been in Ireland (before emigration) or Pennsylvania; search Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (both name-searchable) plus Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable). Window ends 1850 because the 1850 census already places the family.

Patrick's own marriage record (and any earlier marriage) usually names his parents or at least his age and birthplace; Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 is name-searchable, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and church registers cover earlier years. Supplies the next end-of-life evidence given his baptism may be out of reach.

The tree already cites the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses for the Thomas-Patrick link (S1, S2); the 1850 census names every household member and gives birthplace, but not relationship. Add 1870 and 1880 (1880 records relationship to head and parents' birthplaces) and 1900 (birth month/year, immigration year) to follow Thomas, Patrick and any siblings or a mother, and check whether the 1850 household member is really a child of Thomas. Covers the later part of the window to Patrick's death. Also check on the external Schuylkill census collection.

Baptism of Patrick if born in Pennsylvania, from Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable), with variant spellings Flinn, Flynn, Flin, O'Flynn, Patk. Catholic registers are held at the parish or Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001). If the family emigrated, the Irish Catholic baptism ~1845 is held by the National Library of Ireland and other Irish repositories (civil registration there started 1864); the researcher would need to find those on the archive's own site. Consider a full-text co-occurrence search of Thomas and Patrick with sibling names if indexed search stalls.

Probate of Thomas Flynn (born ~1818; could die until ~1900, so window is sized to his lifespan, not Patrick's) at the Schuylkill Register of Wills (from 1811). Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of county wills and administrations. Heirs named would be direct evidence of parentage and name siblings and the mother. Also check an estate for Patrick (d. 1908) listing his parents as heirs or predeceased.

FAN item: naturalization of Thomas Flynn and of Irish neighbors or relatives in the 1850 household vicinity, plus siblings' marriages and baptisms naming the same parents. Naturalizations state origin, arrival and sometimes family; coal-region naturalization films are browse-only image groups (loc_001), so browse image by image. Reveals Thomas's Irish origin parish, pointing to the Irish baptism.

Sweden, Marriages, 1630-1920 (1520596) is name-searchable; try variants Elena/Helena/Lena/Elin and Asmundsdotter/Asmundsdr/Åsmundsdotter. Then verify on the register image, browse-only (personCount 0) in Malmöhus Church Records (1974200); loc_002 lists image groups 004523021 and 004523018.

Her birth falls roughly 1680-1692 (marriage 1712, child 1718). loc_002: Västra Karaby baptism register begins 1688, so a birth before 1688 has no entry; the 1688-1692 part of the window can be searched. Sweden, Baptisms, 1611-1920 (1520594) is name-searchable; then browse the register images (browse-only, personCount 0, groups 004523021/004523018) year by year for an Elena daughter of Asmund.

The baptism may not exist: Västra Karaby's register starts 1688 and her birth may predate it, and her birth parish is unknown. So plan her own death/burial entry. The couple later lived in Barseböck (son Asmund christened there 1718, died there 1768), so she probably died there after 1718; burial entries usually state age and often birthplace. Sweden, Burials, 1649-1920 (1520597) is name-searchable but partial; Barseböck registers (1974200, groups 004514823/004514824) are browse-only (personCount 0), browse by year. Her husband's burial and any remarriage should be checked too.

Dedicated item for her parents' marriage to each other (Asmund and her mother, a candidate Asmund not yet identified; patronymic alone does not say which Asmund). It would confirm them as a couple, give the mother's name, and by date relative to her birth corroborate parentage. It does not itself prove Elena is their child; that needs a record placing her with them (baptism, a household list or probate). Start in Västra Karaby and nearby parishes; registers begin 1688, so earlier marriages may be missing. Use name-searchable Sweden, Marriages (1520596), then browse-only images (1974200).

FAN item: baptisms of the couple's children, starting with Asmund (christened 11 Sep 1718, Barseböck, per tree). Sponsors (godparents) are often her kin and may name her parents or a brother; the child's name Asmund fits Swedish custom of naming a son after the mother's father (Sweden_Naming_Customs, fetched), a lead only. Browse-only (personCount 0) Barseböck registers in 1974200; also check Hofterup, filmed in the same groups.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region.
